---
title: "Ordinal mixed models"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

An ordinal response has categories with a known order but no measured distance between adjacent categories. In MegaVeridicality, *no* is below *maybe*, and *maybe* is below *yes*, but we have no basis for assuming that the two steps are equally large. Recall that [ordinal regression](ordinal-regression.qmd) handles this measurement with a cumulative response family. An [**ordinal mixed model**](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/articles/brms_families.html) combines that response family with [group deviations](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd) for recurring respondents and verbs.

The [expected value](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) of numeric category codes would depend on unsupported distances, so this model instead targets cumulative category probabilities. The [group variation framework](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) supplies respondent and verb deviations. Each response remains one ordered task judgment.

We first make the task and analysis subset concrete. We then build the cumulative model from the three response categories, fit respondent and verb variation, and state exactly which group deviations enter each prediction.

We use **MegaVeridicality v1**, the *no*, *maybe*, and *yes* veridicality judgments described by White and Rawlins ([2018 LingBuzz entry](https://lingbuzz.net/lingbuzz/004012)) and distributed through the [official MegaVeridicality project](https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/). Each row records one respondent's judgment of a low-content, active sentence containing a clause-embedding verb in a *that* clause. The direct task asks whether the embedded event happened after an assertion; the conditional task places that assertion in a conditional antecedent.

The prepared table does not retain sentence strings or a separate stimulus-item
identifier. It retains the verb, frame, voice, polarity, and task. We can thus
identify the recorded **stimulus condition** as a combination of those fields,
but we cannot tell whether rows with the same combination displayed the same
exact sentence wording. The recurring linguistic unit in the model is the verb,
and the verb folds hold out whole verbs. Any claim about variation across exact
sentence items would require an item identifier that this table does not contain.

The two tasks recruited separate samples. Numeric participant labels recur across tasks, so the task label is included when constructing `respondent_id`. Treating repeated numbers as the same people would invent a dependence relation that was not part of the study.

## A fixed analysis subset

```{r}
#| label: prepare-megaveridicality-subset
data_path <- paste0(
  "data/megaveridicality/",
  "megaveridicality-v1-active-native.csv"
)
fold_path <- "data/megaveridicality/verb-folds.csv"
analysis_fold <- 1L

full_judgments <- read.csv(
  data_path,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
verb_folds <- read.csv(
  fold_path,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

judgments <- merge(
  full_judgments,
  verb_folds,
  by = "verb",
  all.x = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(judgments) == 14951L,
  !anyNA(judgments$fold)
)

# Select whole verbs using the preassigned, outcome-blind fold.
judgments <- judgments[judgments$fold == analysis_fold, ]
row.names(judgments) <- NULL
```

The full active and native speaker table contains `r nrow(full_judgments)` responses from
`r length(unique(full_judgments$verb))` active-frame verbs. We begin with the
`r nrow(judgments)` responses for the
`r length(unique(judgments$verb))` verbs assigned to fold
`r analysis_fold`, using a deterministic partition of verb labels created
before their responses were read. This subset lets us work through the response
model and its polarity by task contrasts in fold `r analysis_fold`. The
[prediction for unseen verbs](aspectual-similarity-example.qmd) repeats the procedure across the
complete held out verb comparison.

The partition selected whole verbs without consulting their responses and retained all respondents represented in those rows. The verbs did not enter through probability sampling from the English lexicon, so the estimates describe the verbs and respondents in this fold. The response remains the raw ordered judgment, whereas White and Rawlins analyze normalized participant thresholds and derived measures of veridicality, factivity, and responsivity.

Sentence strings are unavailable in this table, so we work with the recorded task, polarity, verb, frame, respondent, and response rather than inventing source items. One direct and one conditional row are:

```{r}
#| label: megaveridicality-direct-conditional-rows
#| echo: true
do.call(rbind, lapply(c("direct", "conditional"), function(task_value) {
  judgments[judgments$task == task_value, ][1L,
    c("verb", "frame", "polarity", "task", "respondent_id", "response")]
}))
```

## Retaining the ordered response

We can see the cumulative calculation in the observed positive and direct responses from the selected verb fold:

```{r}
#| label: megaveridicality-observed-cumulative-probabilities
ordinal_example <- judgments[
  judgments$polarity == "positive" & judgments$task == "direct",
]
ordinal_example_probability <- prop.table(table(
  factor(
    ordinal_example$response,
    levels = c("no", "maybe", "yes")
  )
))
data.frame(
  response = names(ordinal_example_probability),
  probability = as.numeric(ordinal_example_probability),
  cumulative_probability = cumsum(as.numeric(ordinal_example_probability))
)
```

The first cumulative value is the observed probability of *no*. The second adds the probabilities of *no* and *maybe*. Subtracting the first cumulative value from the second recovers the observed probability of *maybe*, while one minus the second recovers the observed probability of *yes*. This subtraction is the basic operation behind the three category formulas below.

For response $Y_i$ and cutpoint $c$, the cumulative logit model is

$$
\operatorname{logit}\mathbb{P}(Y_i\le c)
=\kappa_c-m_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.
$$

The quantity $m_i$ is the fitted location for response $i$ on the log odds scale:

$$
 m_i
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_{v[i]}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b_{v[i]}
+u_{r[i]}.
$$

The fixed part contains polarity, task, and their interaction. Verbs receive correlated intercept, polarity-slope, and task-slope deviations; respondents receive intercept deviations. For verb $v$ and respondent $r$,

$$
\mathbf b_v\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_v),
\qquad
u_r\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_r^2).
$$

With logistic cumulative distribution $F$, the three category probabilities are

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-m_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{maybe})
=F(\kappa_2-m_i)-F(\kappa_1-m_i),
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-m_i).
$$

The ordered thresholds preserve category order without assigning equal numerical spacing to the labels.

The inequalities $\kappa_1<\kappa_2$ ensure that the probability for *maybe* is
nonnegative. To prepare for the likelihood, let
$q_{ic}(\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf b,
\mathbf u)$ denote the appropriate one of these three probabilities for category
$c$. If response $i$ has observed category $y_i$, its conditional likelihood
contribution is $q_{i,y_i}$. Multiplying over responses gives

$$
p(\mathbf y
\mid
\mathbf b,\mathbf u,
\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\prod_i
q_{i,y_i}
(\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf b,\mathbf u).
$$

This expression uses the probability of the category that was actually
recorded. For instance, an observed *maybe* contributes the difference between
the two cumulative probabilities, rather than either cumulative probability by
itself.

Each selected verb occurs in all four polarity by task cells, so both contrasts vary within verbs and can support slopes by verb. Respondents belong to only one task sample, so a respondent task slope is not identified. We include respondent intercepts and verb slopes, leaving respondent polarity slopes and threshold variation for models with stronger support within respondents or a different account of response style.

The group distributions supply the other part of the joint density. There is
one three-dimensional normal density for each verb and one univariate normal
density for each respondent:

$$
p(\mathbf b,\mathbf u
\mid\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r)
=
\prod_v
\phi_3(\mathbf b_v;\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_v)
\prod_r
\phi(u_r;0,\tau_r^2).
$$

Multiplying the category likelihood by these Gaussian densities gives the joint
density for the observed responses and the unobserved group deviations. The
likelihood for the thresholds, population coefficients, and variance parameters
then integrates out every verb and respondent deviation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(&\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta,
\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r;\mathbf y)\\
&=
\int
p(\mathbf y
\mid\mathbf b,\mathbf u,
\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta)
p(\mathbf b,\mathbf u
\mid\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r)
\,d\mathbf b\,d\mathbf u.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the [general GLMM integral](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd#from-the-conditional-model-to-the-likelihood) with ordered-category contributions in place of Bernoulli contributions. It also shows why fitting cannot consist of choosing a separate best intercept and slope for every verb and respondent. Their possible deviations must be weighted by the Gaussian group densities and then integrated out.

We can now write the objective that `clmm()` will approximate. Collect every
verb and respondent deviation into one $d$-dimensional vector
$\mathbf a=(\mathbf b^{\mathsf T},\mathbf u^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}$ and define

$$
\begin{aligned}
h(&\mathbf a;
\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta,
\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r)\\
&=
\log p(\mathbf y
\mid\mathbf b,\mathbf u,
\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta)
+\log p(\mathbf b,\mathbf u
\mid\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r).
\end{aligned}
$$

For a particular set of thresholds, population coefficients, and variance
parameters, let $\widehat{\mathbf a}$ maximize this log integrand. Let

$$
\mathbf H
=
-\left.
\frac{\partial^2 h(\mathbf a;
\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta,
\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r)}
{\partial\mathbf a\,\partial\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}}
\right|_{\mathbf a=\widehat{\mathbf a}}
$$

record its curvature with respect to all verb and respondent deviations. The
Laplace objective is then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log L(&\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta,
\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r;\mathbf y)\\
&\approx
h(\widehat{\mathbf a};
\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\beta,
\boldsymbol\Sigma_v,\tau_r)
+\frac d2\log(2\pi)
-\frac12\log|\mathbf H|.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus a change to a threshold, a population coefficient, or a variance parameter
requires a new inner calculation of the group deviations and curvature before
the outer optimizer can compare objective values. The [observed-data Laplace
check](laplace-approximation.qmd#constructing-the-supertelicity-integrand) makes
the corresponding contribution, mode, and curvature calculations explicit in
one dimension.

## Fitting the verb-and-respondent model

The fitting call below contains three numerical settings that should not appear without explanation. A **gradient** records the first derivatives of the objective; near an optimum, those derivatives should be close to zero, so `gradTol` declares how close is close enough for the convergence check. A **Hessian** is a matrix of second derivatives that records local curvature in several parameter directions. The earlier discussion of [curvature](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature) shows why its inverse is used to approximate uncertainty. We set `Hess = TRUE` so that we can inspect that curvature rather than trusting an optimizer code alone. The random effect integral above is evaluated with the [Laplace approximation](laplace-approximation.qmd), requested by `nAGQ = 1`. At each candidate set of thresholds, coefficients, and variance parameters, the inner calculation updates the conditional modes and their curvature; the outer optimizer then compares the resulting approximate marginal likelihoods.

```{r}
#| label: fit-megaveridicality-clmm
library(ordinal)
library(ggplot2)

judgments$outcome <- ordered(
  judgments$response,
  levels = c("no", "maybe", "yes")
)
judgments$polarity <- factor(
  judgments$polarity,
  levels = c("positive", "negative")
)
judgments$task <- factor(
  judgments$task,
  levels = c("direct", "conditional")
)
judgments$verb <- factor(judgments$verb)
judgments$respondent_id <- factor(judgments$respondent_id)

cell_counts <- xtabs(
  ~ verb + polarity + task,
  data = judgments
)

direct_ids <- unique(
  judgments$respondent_id[judgments$task == "direct"]
)
conditional_ids <- unique(
  judgments$respondent_id[judgments$task == "conditional"]
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(judgments) == 2990L,
  nlevels(judgments$verb) == 75L,
  nlevels(judgments$respondent_id) == 319L,
  length(direct_ids) == 159L,
  length(conditional_ids) == 160L,
  length(intersect(direct_ids, conditional_ids)) == 0L,
  length(cell_counts) == 300L,
  all(cell_counts > 0L),
  identical(
    sort(as.integer(cell_counts)),
    c(rep(9L, 10L), rep(10L, 290L))
  ),
  all(
    xtabs(~ task + polarity + outcome, data = judgments) > 0L
  )
)

model_formula <- outcome ~ polarity * task +
  (1 + polarity + task | verb) +
  (1 | respondent_id)

fit <- clmm(
  model_formula,
  data = judgments,
  link = "logit",
  Hess = TRUE,
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = clmm.control(
    maxIter = 100L,
    gradTol = 1e-3
  )
)

fit_covariance <- vcov(fit)
fit_hessian_eigenvalues <- eigen(
  fit$Hessian,
  symmetric = TRUE,
  only.values = TRUE
)$values
fit_diagnostics <- c(
  optimizer_code = fit$optRes$convergence,
  maximum_absolute_gradient = max(abs(fit$gradient)),
  smallest_hessian_eigenvalue = min(fit_hessian_eigenvalues),
  covariance_inverse_curvature_difference = max(abs(
    fit_covariance - solve(fit$Hessian)
  ))
)

stopifnot(
  fit_diagnostics[["optimizer_code"]] == 0,
  fit_diagnostics[["maximum_absolute_gradient"]] < 1e-3,
  fit_diagnostics[["smallest_hessian_eigenvalue"]] > 0,
  fit_diagnostics[["covariance_inverse_curvature_difference"]] < 1e-8
)

fit_diagnostics

data_summary <- c(
  judgments = nrow(judgments),
  verbs = nlevels(judgments$verb),
  task_specific_respondents = nlevels(judgments$respondent_id),
  verb_polarity_task_cells = nrow(unique(
    judgments[c("verb", "polarity", "task")]
  ))
)
data_summary
```

The `clmm` arguments map directly to assumptions and computation:

| Argument | Role |
|---|---|
| `outcome ~ polarity * task` | common location effects and their interaction |
| `(1 + polarity + task \| verb)` | correlated verb intercept, polarity slope, and task slope |
| `(1 \| respondent_id)` | respondent location intercept |
| `link = "logit"` | logistic cumulative distribution and proportional-odds location shift |
| `nAGQ = 1` | Laplace approximation to random effect integration |
| `gradTol`, `maxIter` | convergence tolerance and iteration budget, not model assumptions |
| `Hess = TRUE` | retain local curvature for the convergence and covariance checks |

The zero optimizer code and small maximum gradient tell us that the outer
search reached a point whose derivatives are near zero under the stated
tolerance. A Hessian eigenvalue records curvature along one direction
determined by the Hessian. The positive eigenvalues show that the approximate negative log
likelihood bends upward in every fitted parameter direction at that point. Finally, the direct
matrix comparison confirms that `vcov()` is the inverse local curvature of this
approximate marginal objective. These checks support the numerical solution;
they do not remove the Laplace approximation from the likelihood.

The threshold and population coefficient estimates are computed directly from the raw ordered responses:

```{r}
#| label: megaveridicality-clmm-parameters
data.frame(
  parameter = c(names(fit$alpha), names(fit$beta)),
  type = c(
    rep("Threshold", length(fit$alpha)),
    rep("Fixed effect", length(fit$beta))
  ),
  estimate = c(unname(fit$alpha), unname(fit$beta)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

These values are approximate maximum likelihood estimates under the Laplace
objective. They describe the fitted location shifts and group variation for the
analyzed responses. The model contains no latent-category variable or decision
rule that would partition clause-embedding verbs into a taxonomy.

## Checking the approximation with one random intercept

The fitted scientific model has correlated verb slopes and respondent
intercepts, so `clmm()` cannot replace its high-dimensional integral with
high-order quadrature. We can check the same ordered responses under a reduced
model containing one verb intercept. That model gives a one-dimensional integral
for each verb. Adaptive quadrature replaces each integral with a weighted sum
of integrand values placed around its conditional mode, and nine points record
more of the integrand's shape than the local Laplace calculation. This permits
both a Laplace fit and a nine-point adaptive quadrature fit.

```{r}
#| label: megaveridicality-reduced-quadrature-check
reduced_formula <- outcome ~ polarity * task + (1 | verb)
reduced_control <- clmm.control(
  maxIter = 100L,
  gradTol = 5e-3
)

reduced_laplace <- clmm(
  reduced_formula,
  data = judgments,
  link = "logit",
  Hess = TRUE,
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = reduced_control
)

reduced_quadrature <- clmm(
  reduced_formula,
  data = judgments,
  link = "logit",
  Hess = TRUE,
  nAGQ = 9L,
  control = reduced_control
)

reduced_check <- data.frame(
  calculation = c("Laplace", "Nine-point adaptive quadrature"),
  log_likelihood = c(
    as.numeric(logLik(reduced_laplace)),
    as.numeric(logLik(reduced_quadrature))
  ),
  maximum_absolute_gradient = c(
    max(abs(reduced_laplace$gradient)),
    max(abs(reduced_quadrature$gradient))
  ),
  optimizer_code = c(
    reduced_laplace$optRes$convergence,
    reduced_quadrature$optRes$convergence
  )
)

reduced_parameter_difference <- max(abs(
  c(reduced_laplace$alpha, reduced_laplace$beta) -
    c(reduced_quadrature$alpha, reduced_quadrature$beta)
))
reduced_standard_deviation_difference <- abs(
  reduced_laplace$ST[[1L]][1L, 1L] -
    reduced_quadrature$ST[[1L]][1L, 1L]
)

stopifnot(
  all(reduced_check$optimizer_code == 0),
  all(reduced_check$maximum_absolute_gradient < 5e-3),
  reduced_parameter_difference < 0.01,
  reduced_standard_deviation_difference < 0.01
)

reduced_check
c(
  largest_threshold_or_fixed_effect_difference =
    reduced_parameter_difference,
  verb_standard_deviation_difference =
    reduced_standard_deviation_difference
)
```

The higher-order calculation gives a slightly larger log likelihood because it
retains more information about the shape of each integral. The threshold,
fixed effect, and verb standard deviation estimates remain close in the reduced
model. This check concerns one verb intercept on the analyzed responses. It
does not establish that the Laplace approximation is exact for the full verb
slope and respondent intercept model.

## Comparing observed and fitted category probabilities

The fitted points below set verb and respondent deviations to zero. The bars are raw response proportions from the same analysis subset and polarity by task cells. Thus the figure compares raw and fitted quantities from the same `r nlevels(judgments$verb)` verbs.

```{r}
#| label: plot-megaveridicality-clmm
raw_probabilities <- as.data.frame(table(
  judgments$polarity,
  judgments$task,
  judgments$outcome,
  dnn = c("polarity", "task", "response")
))
names(raw_probabilities)[names(raw_probabilities) == "Freq"] <- "responses"
raw_probabilities$probability <- ave(
  raw_probabilities$responses,
  raw_probabilities$polarity,
  raw_probabilities$task,
  FUN = function(x) x / sum(x)
)

prediction_cells <- expand.grid(
  polarity = factor(
    c("positive", "negative"),
    levels = levels(judgments$polarity)
  ),
  task = factor(
    c("direct", "conditional"),
    levels = levels(judgments$task)
  )
)

fixed_matrix <- model.matrix(
  ~ polarity * task,
  data = prediction_cells
)
location <- drop(
  fixed_matrix[, names(fit$beta), drop = FALSE] %*% fit$beta
)
cumulative_probability <- plogis(outer(
  location,
  fit$alpha,
  function(m, threshold) threshold - m
))
category_probability <- cbind(
  cumulative_probability[, 1L],
  cumulative_probability[, 2L] - cumulative_probability[, 1L],
  1 - cumulative_probability[, 2L]
)
colnames(category_probability) <- levels(judgments$outcome)

fitted_probabilities <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(prediction_cells)), function(row) {
    data.frame(
      polarity = prediction_cells$polarity[[row]],
      task = prediction_cells$task[[row]],
      response = factor(
        levels(judgments$outcome),
        levels = levels(judgments$outcome),
        ordered = TRUE
      ),
      probability = category_probability[row, ]
    )
  })
)

ggplot(raw_probabilities, aes(x = response)) +
  geom_col(
    aes(y = probability),
    width = 0.68,
    fill = "grey80",
    color = "grey45"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = fitted_probabilities,
    aes(y = probability),
    color = "#1F5A85",
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  facet_grid(task ~ polarity) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Veridicality response", y = "Response probability") +
  theme_classic()
```

## Stating which groups are represented in a prediction

A prediction for an observed respondent and verb can condition on both estimated deviations. A prediction for a new respondent judging an observed verb may condition on the verb deviation but cannot reuse an observed respondent effect. A prediction for a new respondent and new verb must handle both group distributions.

Setting both deviations to zero gives a location at the center of the distributions on the log odds scale, as in the figure. Averaging category probabilities over either distribution generally produces different probabilities on the response scale because the inverse cumulative logit transformation is nonlinear. A reported probability must thus state which groups are represented in the target.

## What the fitted location can and cannot represent

A positive location shift moves probability toward higher ordered responses. It changes category probabilities; it does not add a fixed number of slider points.

The verb random slopes allow the polarity and task associations to vary across observed verbs. The respondent random intercept allows overall response location to vary across respondents. It cannot represent every response style: respondents might also differ in threshold spacing or in how often they use *maybe*. A location-intercept model leaves those possibilities outside its structure.

White and Rawlins normalize responses and study derived veridicality, factivity, responsivity, and clause-selection patterns. We instead analyze raw ordered responses as a function of polarity and task so that the cumulative-link and random effect assumptions are visible on the recorded scale. The resulting coefficients answer that narrower question and do not reproduce the paper's normalization or responsivity analysis.

## Recap and check

1. What does proportional odds assume? A predictor shifts one location $m_i$ across both cumulative cutpoints; it does not receive a separate coefficient at each threshold.
2. Can an observed-verb conditional mode be used for a new verb? No. A new verb has no estimated deviation; its prediction must use zero deviations or average over the verb distribution.
3. Which observations do these estimates describe? They describe the
   respondents and verbs represented in fold 1, under the recorded polarity and
   task conditions. They do not estimate variation across exact sentence items,
   because the prepared table has no sentence-item identifier. The
   discussion of [unseen verbs](aspectual-similarity-example.qmd) carries out the complete
   held out verb comparison.

We next ask whether the fixed interaction predicts judgments for [verbs absent from fitting](aspectual-similarity-example.qmd).
